rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Bohr explained the hydrogen line spectrum: electrons occupy quantised orbits Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n², and light is emitted only in downward jumps, each photon carrying exactly the gap (hν = E₂ − E₁). The Rydberg equation 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, predicts five series named for their lower level: Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV), Balmer (n₁ = 2, the only visible series — Hα 656.3 nm, Hβ 486.1 nm), Paschen, Brackett and…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n² = −13.6 eV / n² - hν = E₂ − E₁ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) J - 1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ - λ = hc/ΔE; series limit λ = n₁²/R - Hydrogen-like ions: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Orbit vs jump:** energy is *possessed* in an orbit but *radiated only during a jump* between orbits — the orbit itself emits nothing.  ·  **n₁ vs n₂:** in the Rydberg equation n₁ is the **lower (final)** level and n₂ the **upper (initial)** level; reversing them gives a negative result.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Each line of the hydrogen spectrum corresponds to one definite electronic jump between two quantised orbits."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Hα = 656.3 nm*** — the 3 → 2 Balmer jump; the same ΔE (3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) computed from Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J lands on exactly this wavelength.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Fingerprint That Saved Bohr Rutherford's model could not explain why atomic hydrogen emits **discrete coloured lines** instead of a continuous glow. Bohr (1913) turned that failure into a triumph: if electrons occupy only **quantised orbits**, an electron dropping from a higher orbit to a lower one emits a photon carrying exactly the energy gap — hν = E₂ − E₁.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Energy of the nth orbit - Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n² = **−13.6 eV / n²** (n = 1, 2, 3, …). - The **negative sign** means the electron is bound; E₁ = −13.6 eV is the **ground state**, E∞ = 0 is **ionisation**. - Energy gaps shrink as n grows — levels crowd together near the ionisation limit.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "1-2-3-4-5 → Lyman-Balmer-Paschen-Brackett-Pfund; UV-Visible-IR-IR-IR." Series limit = 1/(R·n₁²).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2022 (3m): Using Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J, calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of a hydrogen atom and the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron falls from the third to the second orbit (in nm).** — E₂ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/4 = **−5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Name the five spectral series of hydrogen with their lower levels and regions.** — Lyman (n₁ = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (n₁ = 2, visible), Paschen (n₁ = 3, infrared), Brackett (n₁ = 4, infrared), Pfund (n₁ = 5, far infrared). Only Balmer lies in the visible region.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always compute ΔE first, then λ = hc/ΔE; quote λ in nm for NEB (656 nm, not 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m alone). Keep 3 significant figures.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Quantisation → line spectrum:** fixed level gaps give fixed photon energies; each line is one transition, which is why spectra are element fingerprints.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n²; photon rule hν = E₂ − E₁; Rydberg 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Five series: Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV, limit 91.2 nm), Balmer (n₁ = 2, visible, limit 364.6 nm), Paschen (n₁ = 3), Brackett (n₁ = 4), Pfund (n₁ = 5) — all infrared.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe (~75% by mass), so its Balmer lines dominate visible stellar spectra — Hα is how astronomers map nebulae and solar chromosphere.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): What is the ionisation energy of hydrogen in eV and joule?** — Ionisation takes the electron from n = 1 to n = ∞: ΔE = 0 − (−13.6 eV) = **13.6 eV = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J** (the magnitude of E₁).  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Distinguish emission and absorption spectra with one example each.** — Emission: excited atoms emit photons on downward jumps — bright lines on dark background (hydrogen discharge tube).…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | **Line spectrum** | Discrete wavelengths emitted by excited atoms, each from one defined transition | Evidence of quantised energy levels | | **Ground state** | Lowest orbit n = 1, E = −13.6 eV | Normal state of hydrogen | | **Excited state** | Any orbit n > 1 | Reached by absorbing…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why lines, not a rainbow Classical physics: an orbiting electron radiates continuously, spirals inward, and the spectrum should be continuous. Bohr: orbits are **stationary** — no radiation while the electron stays put.…  ·  ### Deep dive — the five series as one formula with a moving target Every hydrogen line obeys 1/λ = R_H (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. The series differ only in which level the electron *lands on* (n₁): - **Lyman** (n₁ = 1, UV): discovered 1906; the series limit at 91.2 nm corresponds to ionisation from the ground state — 13.6 eV exactly.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 5. Comparison Tables **Emission vs absorption spectrum** | Basis | Emission spectrum | Absorption spectrum | |---|---|---| | Source | Excited atoms releasing energy | Cool gas removing energy from white light | | Appearance | Bright lines on dark background | Dark lines on continuous background | | Electron jump |…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Series limit vs first line:** the limit (n₂ → ∞) is the *shortest* wavelength; the first line (smallest gap, e.g. 3 → 2) is the *longest* — students swap them.  ·  **Balmer vs Lyman direction:** Lyman needs jumps **down to n = 1** (from any higher level); Balmer needs jumps **down to n = 2**. A 3 → 2 jump is Balmer even though it starts at n = 3.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Rydberg sign convention:** 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with n₁ the **lower** level; writing the terms the other way gives a negative 1/λ — physically meaningless.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **NEB-style (2m): Why does hydrogen produce a line spectrum rather than a continuous spectrum?** Because Bohr orbits are quantised and stationary: radiation is emitted only in jumps between fixed levels, so each photon has one definite energy — discrete lines, not a continuum.  ·  ```svg The hydrogen spectrum — five series, one landing level each <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" font-family="Segoe UI" font-size="13"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><g stroke="#111827" stroke-width="2"><line x1="100" y1="60" x2="560" y2="60"/><line x1="100" y1="110" x2="560" y2="110"/><line…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Calculate the wavelength of the Hα line (3 → 2).** 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ (1/4 − 1/9) = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 5/36 = 1.524 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ → λ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m = **656.3 nm**.  ·  **NEB-style (3m): The second line of the Balmer series (4 → 2).** 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ (1/4 − 1/16) = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 3/16 → λ = **486.1 nm** (Hβ, blue-green).
